# requestAnimationFrame ⏱️

#### Course: Brick Breaker with JavaScript

## requestAnimationFrame ⏱️

The ball is sitting still on screen.

That's because nothing is telling it to move yet.

To make a game run, you need a loop. Something that calls update and draw over and over, as fast as the browser can handle. That's what requestAnimationFrame does. You give it a function and it calls that function just before the browser paints the next frame. Roughly 60 times per second.

The pattern looks like this:

```javascriptDOM
loop() {
  this.update();   // advance game state
  this.draw();     // render current state

  requestAnimationFrame(this.loop);  // schedule next frame
}

start() {
  requestAnimationFrame(this.loop);  // kick it off
}
```

Before you use this, there is one thing that will silently break it. When requestAnimationFrame calls this.loop, it loses track of what this refers to. The loop stops with no error and no hint of why.

Fix it in the constructor before anything else:

```javascriptDOM
constructor(canvasElement) {
  // Bind first, before any other setup
  this.loop = this.loop.bind(this);
  // ... rest of constructor
}
```

That line makes sure this always points to your Game instance no matter who calls the function.

![Animation Loop](data:application/octet-stream;base64,)

Next, you will give the ball a velocity and make it move across the canvas.
